title: Flexor tendon injury in the hand

guidelineVersions: BSSH Trauma Standards: Lacerations with Flexor Tendon Involvement (British Society for Surgery of the Hand)
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition (2023)

related.why: Flexor sheath infection: shares the flexor sheath/tendon anatomy and urgent hand-surgery referral pathway
Applied anatomy of the hand (median and ulnar nerves, carpal tunnel), relevant to associated nerve injury

brief.scenario: Mr Yusuf Bramley, 26, has cut his palm on broken glass and cannot flex his ring finger normally.
brief.task: Examine him, identify the structures at risk, and explain your management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Circulation and sensation first, then isolated FDP/FDS testing, then wound assessment, then urgent specialist referral.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Assuming a normal-looking fist means the tendons are intact, or that any doctor can repair the tendon in the emergency department.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess circulation, sensation and motor function before examining the wound itself."

flow: Inspect the wound for associated structures
Urgent specialist referral and explain the plan

grid.label: General assessment before the wound
grid.fail: Goes straight to inspecting the wound without first assessing circulation, sensation and motor function.
grid.pass: Assesses circulation, sensation and motor function first.
grid.high: Compares active flexion of the relevant joints individually with the other hand before drawing conclusions.

grid.label: Isolated FDP and FDS testing
grid.fail: Only asks him to make a fist, without testing FDP and FDS individually.
grid.pass: Assesses both FDP and FDS function individually, because isolated testing can identify which tendon is injured.
grid.high: Describes the technique: hold other joints extended and flex the distal interphalangeal joint to isolate FDP; hold adjacent fingers extended to isolate FDS.

grid.label: Inspect for associated structures
grid.fail: Closes the skin and arranges review without assessing for associated digital nerve, artery or other tendon injury.
grid.pass: Inspects the wound and assesses for associated digital nerve, artery and other tendon injuries.
grid.high: Explains that the digital nerves run close to the flexor tendons and can be injured simultaneously, so sensation is tested specifically over each digital nerve distribution.

grid.label: Imaging when indicated
grid.fail: States that an X-ray alone is enough to exclude significant injury.
grid.pass: Obtains imaging if there is concern about a retained foreign body or fracture.
grid.high: Specifies that imaging is targeted to that concern (foreign body or fracture) rather than ordered routinely for every hand laceration.

grid.label: Urgent specialist referral (safety-critical)
grid.fail: States that any doctor can repair the tendon in the emergency department.
grid.pass: Refers urgently to a specialist hand service, explaining that a divided flexor tendon generally requires specialist repair and structured postoperative hand therapy.
grid.high: States repair is undertaken by a competent flexor tendon surgeon and that rehabilitation with a hand therapist is planned from the outset, not added later.

failures.move: Testing tendon function only by asking him to make a fist.
failures.consequence: An isolated FDP or FDS injury can be missed because the other tendon compensates.

failures.move: Closing the skin and arranging review without assessing for associated nerve, artery or other tendon injury.
failures.consequence: A concurrent digital nerve or artery injury is missed and treatment is delayed.

failures.move: Attempting or allowing tendon repair in the emergency department by a non-specialist.
failures.consequence: Inadequate repair technique risks poor tendon gliding, adhesions and permanent loss of function.

failures.move: Examining the wound before assessing circulation, sensation and motor function.
failures.consequence: A vascular or nerve injury needing urgent attention can be overlooked.

recovery.when: You blank on what to do next
recovery.line: I'd like to structure this around immediate safety, assessment, escalation and definitive management.

recovery.when: Asked "anything else?" after the tendon assessment
recovery.line: Yes — I'd also check for digital nerve and artery injury and involve a specialist hand service urgently.

knowledge.fact: Test FDP by holding the other finger joints extended and asking for distal interphalangeal flexion; test FDS by holding adjacent fingers extended.
Digital nerves run close to the flexor tendons and may be injured at the same time, so sensation is tested specifically.
A divided flexor tendon requires specialist repair by a competent flexor tendon surgeon and structured postoperative hand therapy.
Operative repair is generally within 4 days of injury.

recall.think: Missed isolated tendon or digital nerve/artery injury under a deceptively normal-looking fist.
recall.say: "Assessing circulation, sensation and motor function first, then testing FDP and FDS individually."
do: Refer urgently to specialist hand service

recall.finish: Specialist flexor tendon repair with structured postoperative hand therapy.

partner.opening: Mr Yusuf Bramley, 26, has cut his palm on broken glass and cannot flex his ring finger normally. "Examine him, identify the structures at risk, and explain your management."

reveals.finding: Capillary refill is normal but sensation is reduced over the ulnar aspect of the ring finger.

reveals.trigger: Candidate tests FDP and FDS individually
reveals.finding: FDP flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint is absent; FDS is intact.
A clean laceration across the distal palmar crease with no obvious active bleeding.

push.question: How do you test FDP?
push.expect: Hold the other finger joints extended and ask the patient to flex the distal interphalangeal joint.

push.question: Why test sensation?
push.expect: The digital nerves run close to the flexor tendons and may be injured simultaneously.

push.question: Who should repair this?
push.expect: A specialist hand service with a competent flexor tendon surgeon and planned hand therapy.

curveballs.prompt: A colleague suggests closing the skin now and referring routinely.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — refer urgently to the specialist hand service given the confirmed tendon injury.

curveballs.prompt: He can still make a reasonable fist despite the wound.
curveballs.safeAnswer: A normal-looking fist does not exclude an isolated FDP or FDS injury; test them individually.

curveballs.prompt: There is a small retained fragment of glass suspected in the wound.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Obtain imaging targeted at excluding a retained foreign body before definitive repair.
